interactions.summary: Jiang returns to the Divine Comedy as evidence that a purely material account of genius is insufficient: if God does not exist, he does not understand how Dante alone could build a work of this scale and still communicate beauty and truth to readers a millennium later.

A student asks whether substances such as nicotine or marijuana might temporarily raise human cognitive capacity, and Jiang rejects the easy explanatory move by stressing that even in an age of abundant information and wealth, no modern equivalent of Dante has appeared.

Another student separates literary admiration for Dante from belief in God and objects to exporting divine inspiration into present-day neuroscience; Jiang answers by defining the class as a space for speculation and inquiry rather than doctrinal enforcement.

A student reads Beatrice's distinction between the formal compact of a vow, which cannot simply be annulled, and the matter of a vow, which in some cases may be altered only under proper authority; some vows are so weighty that no substitute can balance them.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that the existence of the Divine Comedy is difficult to explain without God because Dante, working alone over decades and without modern tools, produced a work whose intended truth and beauty remain intelligible almost a thousand years later.
He says contemporary abundance of information and wealth has still not produced another Dante, which for him deepens rather than solves the mystery of literary genius.
Jiang frames the classroom as a space of speculation, inquiry, and debate where students may keep their own beliefs even when he pushes metaphysical interpretations.

In the Beatrice passage read aloud here, the formal compact of a vow cannot be annulled at will, some vow-matter may be altered only properly, and certain vows are so weighty that no substitute can stand in for them.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats the Divine Comedy itself as an almost brute fact pointing beyond materialism.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if god doesn't exist i have no idea how this was written
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This condenses his move from literary admiration into metaphysical pressure.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang answers a brain-enhancement question by saying that, compared to Dante, modern people with every advantage still look intellectually diminished.
signature_moments.source_phrase: compared to dante we're all kind of stupid
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The insult preserves the heat of his anti-progress narrative about genius.

signature_moments.moment: He abruptly redefines the class as inquiry rather than proof when a student resists importing divine inspiration into science.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is a class of speculation of inquiry of debate
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows how Jiang preserves metaphysical intensity while keeping the room open to dissent.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The binding form of a vow in Beatrice's account, which cannot simply be revoked at personal discretion.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-18 Jiang moves from arguing that Dante's genius strains materialist explanation to reopening the text's vow logic, while explicitly bracketing the room as a site of speculative argument rather than enforced belief.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's brain-enhancement question is disfluent and likely ASR-distorted, but the core proposal is clear: chemical stimulation might temporarily unlock more brain capacity.
